items.plain: Whatever made poverty hard also makes wealth hard. A sick man is sick on any bed, and a troubled mind stays troubled whether it is rich or poor; the illness travels with the person.
items.core_idea: A troubled mind stays troubled, rich or poor.

items.plain: It takes courage to stay sober while the crowd gets drunk, but more self-control to join in the festival in your own restrained way, neither standing out nor losing yourself in the crowd.
items.core_idea: Join in with the crowd, but on your own terms.

items.plain: Use calm, easy times to toughen your mind for hard ones, as soldiers drill in peacetime. If you don't want someone to flinch in a crisis, train them before it arrives.
items.core_idea: Prepare for hardship while times are good.

items.plain: A fire's damage depends on what it lands on: solid wood resists, dry tinder blazes. Anger works the same way; great anger ends in madness, so avoid anger altogether to keep your mind healthy.
items.core_idea: Avoid anger to keep a healthy mind.

items.plain: In a quieter, private life you would have less but feel full; now you have plenty and are never satisfied. Would you rather be poor and content, or rich and hungry? Wealth is greedy and draws others' greed.
items.core_idea: Better poor and content than rich and hungry.

items.plain: Think harder about who you will eat and drink with than about what you will eat. A meal without a friend is the life of a lion or a wolf.
items.core_idea: Choose your companions more carefully than your food.

items.plain: Don't pick friends among those who come to flatter you. A busy, wealthy man thinks people are his friends when he is no friend to them; a small debt makes someone owe you, a large one makes them hate you.
items.core_idea: Big favours can turn people into enemies.

items.plain: The highest mark of wisdom is that your actions match your words and you stay the same person in every situation. Few manage it, and no philosopher keeps the same pace always, but he can always walk the same path.
items.core_idea: Wisdom means your actions match your words.

items.plain: Choose one standard to live by and run your whole life by it. People who live modestly at home but show off in public reveal an unsteady mind that hasn't found its balance.
items.core_idea: Live by one consistent standard everywhere.

items.plain: Poverty keeps your true friends and clears away those who wanted what you had. You might love it for that alone, since it shows who really loves you. When will no one flatter you with lies?
items.core_idea: Poverty reveals who truly loves you.

items.plain: Nobody is born rich. Every baby must make do with milk and rags; that is how we all start, and yet later whole kingdoms feel too small for us.
items.core_idea: We start with little, then want everything.

items.plain: Your biggest obstacle is yourself. You don't know what you want; you approve the right path more readily than you follow it; you see where real happiness lies but lack the courage to reach it.
items.core_idea: You are your own biggest obstacle.

items.plain: Time will sweep over us all like a flood. A few great people will keep their heads above it for a long while, fighting oblivion, though in the end they too will go into silence.
items.core_idea: Time buries all; a few resist longer.

items.plain: Epicurus said that to make Pythocles rich, you shouldn't give him more money but take away some of his desires.
items.core_idea: Wealth comes from wanting less, not having more.

items.plain: People complain about their ambitions the way lovers complain about each other: it is squabbling, not real hatred. They stay by choice in what they call unbearable. A few are held by slavery; many more cling to it.
items.core_idea: Many people cling to what they claim enslaves them.

items.plain: If you keep looking back to see how much wealth you can take with you into a quieter life, you will never get out. No one can swim to shore carrying their luggage.
items.core_idea: You can't escape while clutching your possessions.

items.plain: Catch anyone unawares, young or old, and you will find them equally afraid of death and equally ignorant of how to live. No one has finished anything, because we keep postponing everything to the future.
items.core_idea: Postponing life leaves us afraid of death.

items.plain: A person has understood wisdom if they can die as free of worry as when they were born. Instead we panic as the end nears, turning pale and weeping uselessly. What is worse than fretting at the doorway of peace?
items.core_idea: Wisdom is dying as calmly as you were born.

items.plain: People care how long they live, not how well, though anyone can choose to live nobly and no one can choose to live long.
items.core_idea: Living nobly is in our power; living long isn't.

items.plain: The foundation, and really the summit, of a sound mind is not taking joy in useless things and not letting outside things control your happiness. Anyone driven by hope for something, however attainable, stays troubled and unsure.
items.core_idea: Don't let external things control your happiness.

items.plain: I want you never to lack gladness, and for it to be born at home, inside you. Other pleasures only smooth the brow for a while; laughing isn't joy. The soul itself must be happy and confident, above every circumstance.
items.core_idea: Real gladness is born inside you.

items.plain: Real good comes from a clear conscience, honourable aims, right actions, indifference to luck, and a calm, steady life on one path. People who jump from one goal to another, or drift by chance, cannot hold any lasting good.
items.core_idea: Lasting good comes from a steady, honest life.

items.plain: Few steer their lives by a clear purpose; the rest drift like things in a river, some gently, some violently, some stranded, some swept out to sea. So decide what you want and stick to it.
items.core_idea: Decide what you want and stick to it.

items.plain: Some people only start living when it's time to stop. More surprising still, some have stopped living before they ever began.
items.core_idea: Some stop living before they ever begin.

items.plain: Why invite trouble early and spoil today by fearing tomorrow? It is foolish to be unhappy now over what might come. Instead, assume what you fear will happen, size it up, and you'll see it is either small or brief.
items.core_idea: Measure your fear; it is smaller than you think.

items.plain: Death is so little to be feared that, thanks to it, there is nothing left to fear at all.
items.core_idea: Because of death, nothing need be feared.

items.plain: Strip things of everything that disturbs and confuses, and see what they really are; you'll find nothing fearful in them but the fear. Like children scared of loved ones in masks, we must take the masks off things.
items.core_idea: Unmask things; often only the fear is frightening.

items.plain: Have you only just realised that death, exile and grief hang over you? You were born into these dangers. Let us treat everything that could happen as something that will happen.
items.core_idea: Expect that whatever can happen will happen.

items.plain: If I become poor, I'll be one of many; if exiled, I'll treat my new place as home; if chained, I'm already bound to a body. Saying 'I shall die' really means I'll no longer risk sickness, prison, or death.
items.core_idea: Feared misfortunes lose their power when examined.

items.plain: We lose childhood, then youth; all past time is gone, and even today is shared with death. As the last drop doesn't empty the water-clock alone, our final hour only completes a dying we've long been doing.
items.core_idea: We are dying a little every day.

items.plain: Epicurus says it is absurd to rush toward death because you're tired of life, when it was your way of living that drove you toward death.
items.core_idea: Weariness of life comes from how we live.

items.plain: I don't know if I'll succeed, but I'd rather lack success than lack faith. Don't give up on curing the sick even when the illness is long-standing, if you resist excess and make them do hard things.
items.core_idea: Better to lack success than lack faith.

items.plain: Act as if Epicurus were watching you. It helps to have someone to look up to as a witness of your thoughts; live as if a good person were beside you, since solitude tempts us to wrongdoing.
items.core_idea: Live as if a good person were watching.

items.plain: Only my vices and what fed them have grown old; my mind is strong and glad to be loosely tied to the body. It has set down most of its load and calls old age its time to bloom.
items.core_idea: In old age, the mind can bloom.

items.plain: Ignore public opinion, which always wavers, and set aside your learning; death will give the final verdict. Your clever talk and gathered maxims prove nothing about your soul's strength. What you truly are shows only at your last breath.
items.core_idea: Your last breath shows your soul's true strength.

items.plain: You are younger, but so what? Our years are not counted out in advance. You don't know where death is waiting for you, so be ready for it everywhere.
items.core_idea: Death may come anywhere; be ready.

items.plain: I'm not so shameless as to try to cure others while I am sick myself. I am discussing troubles we share and passing on the remedy, as if we lay ill in the same hospital.
items.core_idea: We share our troubles as fellow patients.

items.plain: Before you die, make sure your faults die first. Disordered pleasures cost dearly and leave regret. Seek a good that lasts, which the soul can find only within itself; virtue alone gives lasting, peaceful joy, untouched by passing troubles.
items.core_idea: Let your faults die before you do.

items.plain: Do you think you're the only one this has happened to, that all your travel hasn't lifted the heaviness from your mind? What you need is a change of soul, not a change of climate.
items.core_idea: You need a change of soul, not scenery.

items.plain: Socrates asked why travel would help when you always take yourself along. New places are useless if you flee with yourself in tow. Until you put down the burdens of your mind, no place will satisfy you.
items.core_idea: Wherever you go, you take yourself with you.

items.plain: Who you are matters more than where you go, so don't tie your mind to any one place. Live by this: I wasn't born for one corner of the universe; the whole world is my country.
items.core_idea: The whole world is my country.

items.plain: I disagree with those who seek a stormy life and wrestle with problems daily. The wise person endures all that but doesn't choose it, preferring peace to war. Casting out your faults helps little if you then fight others'.
items.core_idea: The wise endure storms but prefer peace.

items.plain: Epicurus said knowing your wrongdoing begins salvation; you can't want correction until you see you're wrong. Rather than boasting of faults, find yourself guilty: be accuser, then judge, then advocate, and sometimes be hard on yourself.
items.core_idea: Admitting your faults is the start of reform.

items.plain: Don't count how many people frighten you. Many may threaten your life, but only one at a time can reach you. Nature has arranged it so that as only one gave you life, only one will take it away.
items.core_idea: Many may threaten, but only one can strike.

items.plain: Winning popular approval takes trickery and making yourself like the crowd. But what you think of yourself matters far more than what others think. The favour of low people can only be won by low means.
items.core_idea: Your own judgment of yourself matters most.

items.plain: Philosophy makes us joyful even facing death, strong and cheerful whatever state the body is in. A great pilot can still sail with torn sails, and keep even a wrecked hull on course.
items.core_idea: A strong mind sails on when the body fails.

items.plain: Leaving calmly when your hour comes takes long practice. Other dangers leave hope: illnesses end, fires go out, people survive. But old age leading toward death grants no reprieve; no ending is gentler, yet none lingers longer.
items.core_idea: Departing calmly in old age takes long practice.

items.plain: Whoever doesn't want to die never truly wanted to live, since life is given on condition of death. It is foolish to fear what is certain. Death's rule is fair and binds everyone; equality is the heart of fairness.
items.core_idea: Life is given on condition of death.

items.plain: An enemy threatens death, but indigestion gets there first. Some fears are real, others only seem so. We fear not death but the thought of it. Death is always equally near, so no time of life is free of it.
items.core_idea: We fear the thought of death, not death.

items.plain: Don't listen to those who love you most; they wish bad things for you with good intentions. If you want to be happy, ask the gods that none of their fond wishes for you come true.
items.core_idea: Loved ones often wish us the wrong things.

items.plain: What are 'Roman knight', 'freedman's son' or 'slave'? Just titles born of ambition or injustice. A person can leap to heaven from the slums.
items.core_idea: Anyone can rise to greatness from any origin.

items.plain: Anyone who holds you back does real harm, since life is short, and we shorten it further by being unsteady, always making fresh starts. We break life into little pieces and fritter it away.
items.core_idea: Constant fresh starts fritter life away.

items.plain: When will you reach the point where time means nothing to you, calm and unconcerned about tomorrow because you are fully enjoying your life? People crave the future because no one has yet found himself.
items.core_idea: We crave the future because we haven't found ourselves.

items.plain: I'll use the old road, but take a shorter, smoother one if I find it. Earlier discoverers are guides, not masters. Truth is open to all, owned by no one, and much remains for future generations.
items.core_idea: Past thinkers are guides, not masters.

items.plain: A friend loves you, but not everyone who loves you is a friend. Friendship always helps; love can sometimes do harm. Work on improving yourself, if only so you learn how to love.
items.core_idea: Not everyone who loves you is your friend.

items.plain: We feel joy about loved ones even when apart, but it is light and brief. Seeing someone, being with them and talking together gives a living pleasure, especially when they are the kind of person you hoped for.
items.core_idea: Being together brings a living joy.

items.plain: Hurry to find me, but find yourself first. Above all, be consistent with yourself. To test your progress, ask whether you want the same things today as yesterday. A shifting will means a mind adrift; what is settled stays put.
items.core_idea: Progress means wanting the same things consistently.

items.plain: Look how the universe repeats its cycle: no star goes out; they set and rise in turn. Summer leaves but returns next year, winter comes back in its months, and night overwhelms the sun only for day to return.
items.core_idea: Everything that sets will rise again.

items.plain: You ask how to free yourself. You can't escape what is necessary, but you can overcome it.
items.core_idea: You can't escape necessity, but you can overcome it.

items.plain: No one knows how they started craving what they crave; impulse, not thought, drove them there. It is shameful to drift instead of moving forward, then suddenly ask, dazed, in the middle of the whirlpool, how you got here.
items.core_idea: Don't drift, then wonder how you got here.

items.plain: Words should be scattered like seed: however small, in good ground they grow great. Reason grows the same way, increasing as it works. Few words are needed; if the mind truly takes them in, they gain strength and spring up.
items.core_idea: A few good words can grow great in the mind.

items.plain: Like a flame, the soul is always moving, and the more eager, the more active. Happy is the one who turns it toward better things: he rises above chance, handles good fortune wisely, eases hardship, and scorns what others admire.
items.core_idea: Direct the soul's restless energy toward better things.

items.plain: A great soul scorns great things and prefers the ordinary to the excessive. Too-rich soil flattens grain and heavy loads break branches; likewise the soul is ruined by unchecked prosperity, which harms both others and itself.
items.core_idea: Excess prosperity ruins the soul.

items.plain: Need sets a limit, but nothing limits luxuries. So people sink into pleasures until what was extra becomes essential, and they become slaves to them. Worst of all is loving your own ills, when vices have become habits beyond cure.
items.core_idea: Luxuries become needs, and then we're enslaved.

items.plain: Thank you for writing so often; your letters show me your real self and bring me straight into your company. If pictures of absent friends please us, a letter, carrying real traces of a friend's hand, pleases far more.
items.core_idea: A friend's letter brings their real presence.

items.plain: No need to raise hands to heaven or beg at temples. God is near you, with you, within you. A holy spirit dwells in us, watching our deeds; as we treat it, it treats us. None is good without God.
items.core_idea: God is near you, with you, within you.

items.plain: If you saw someone fearless in danger, free of cravings, happy in hardship, calm in a storm, wouldn't you feel reverence? You'd say such greatness is too lofty for a small body; a divine power has come upon them.
items.core_idea: A calm, fearless soul seems touched by the divine.

items.plain: Take pride only in what is truly yours. We praise a vine for its fruit, not golden leaves. Slaves, houses and income are outside a person. Praise what can't be given or taken: the soul, and reason perfected in it.
items.core_idea: Praise the soul, not possessions.

items.plain: We think we only 'buy' what we pay cash for, yet we spend our very selves, through anxiety, danger, honour, freedom and time, as if nothing were cheaper than ourselves. Check the true price; often what costs nothing costs most.
items.core_idea: What costs nothing often costs us most.

items.plain: This thing will perish? It was an extra; you'll live without it as before. Whether you had it long or briefly, losing it is bearable. Less money means less trouble; less influence, less envy.
items.core_idea: Every loss also removes a burden.

items.plain: Look at the losses we weep over: what troubles us is not the loss but the idea of loss. Our mind tells us something is gone. Whoever owns himself has lost nothing, but few are blessed with owning themselves.
items.core_idea: Whoever owns himself has lost nothing.

items.plain: A good conscience is happy among crowds; a bad one is troubled even alone. If your deeds are honourable, let everyone know; if shameful, what does secrecy matter when you know? How wretched to scorn that witness.
items.core_idea: You yourself always witness your own deeds.

items.plain: The well-born are those naturally fitted for virtue. Trace any family far enough and its origins are mixed. Ancestral busts don't make a noble; the past isn't ours. Only the soul ennobles us, and it can rise from any condition.
items.core_idea: Only the soul makes a person noble.

items.plain: Everyone wants a happy life but mistakes the means for happiness, fleeing it while seeking it. Happiness is freedom from care, yet people pile up worries. As in a maze, the faster you hurry, the worse you're tangled.
items.core_idea: Chasing happiness's trappings drives it away.

items.plain: Things lead us astray, so we must learn to tell them apart. We embrace bad instead of good and pray for the opposite of what we once prayed for. Our prayers clash with our prayers, our plans with our plans.
items.core_idea: Our desires contradict each other.

items.plain: Flattery looks so like friendship that it outdoes it, welcomed deep into the heart and pleasing exactly where it harms. Enemies come as friends; vices pass for virtues, rashness for bravery, cowardice for prudence. Mistaking them is dangerous.
items.core_idea: Flattery disguises itself as friendship.

items.plain: Everyone lives for tomorrow, and that does great harm: such people don't live, they prepare to live, postponing everything. As it is, life passes us by as if it were someone else's, perishing a little each day.
items.core_idea: Living for tomorrow means never truly living.

items.plain: Treat those below you as you would want those above you to treat you. Whenever you think how much power you have over a slave, remember your master has just as much over you.
items.core_idea: Treat inferiors as you'd want superiors to treat you.

items.plain: Don't seek friends only in public life; look carefully and you'll find them at home. Good material often waits for an artist. Judging a horse by its saddle is foolish; judging a person by clothes or rank is doubly so.
items.core_idea: Don't judge people by their clothes or rank.

items.plain: Show me someone who isn't a slave: to lust, greed, ambition, and all to fear. Ex-consuls, millionaires and nobles are enslaved to others. No slavery is more shameful than the kind we choose for ourselves.
items.core_idea: Self-imposed slavery is the most shameful.

items.plain: What annoys us doesn't necessarily harm us. Our luxurious lives make us fly into rage at anything that doesn't suit our whims.
items.core_idea: Luxury makes small annoyances feel like injuries.

items.plain: One sign of good character is that it forms its own judgments and sticks to them; badness is fickle, always changing, not for the better but just for something different.
items.core_idea: Good character holds steady; badness keeps shifting.

items.plain: Friendship makes all our interests shared; no one's fortune is theirs alone, since we live in common. No one who thinks only of his own advantage can be happy; live for your neighbour if you would live for yourself.
items.core_idea: Live for your neighbour to live for yourself.

items.plain: It is careless to remember a friend only when a landscape reminds you. Yet familiar places can stir a stored-away sense of loss, waking old memories, just as a lost friend's cloak or house renews grief that time had softened.
items.core_idea: Familiar places reawaken grief softened by time.

items.plain: It seems only a moment since I was a schoolboy, a moment since I began pleading in court, then lost the wish and the ability. Time flies incredibly fast, as those looking back see; in the present we barely notice.
items.core_idea: Time flies; we only see it looking back.

items.plain: All past time lies together in one abyss. Life is a point, even less, yet nature makes it seem longer by dividing it into infancy, childhood, youth, middle years and old age. So many steps for so short a climb.
items.core_idea: Life is brief, though its stages make it seem long.

items.plain: Death trails me and life slips away; teach me to face this. Help me stop fleeing death and keep life from fleeing me. Show me life's good lies in its use, not length; many who live long live too little.
items.core_idea: Life's worth lies in its use, not length.

items.plain: Don't think the gap between life and death is narrow only at sea. It is just as narrow everywhere. Death doesn't show itself as close everywhere, but everywhere it is just as close.
items.core_idea: Death is equally near everywhere.

items.plain: Why fool ourselves? Our trouble is not outside us but deep within, and healing is harder because we don't even know we are sick.
items.core_idea: Our trouble is within, and we don't see it.

items.plain: Everything yields to steady, careful treatment; bent timber can be straightened, and heat reshapes curved beams. How much more easily the soul can be shaped, since it is more pliable than any liquid.
items.core_idea: With patient effort, the soul can be reshaped.

items.plain: Don't lose hope for us because we're caught in evil, even for a long time. No one gets a good mind before a bad one; the bad takes hold of us first. Learning virtue means unlearning vice.
items.core_idea: Learning virtue means unlearning vice.

items.plain: What force drags us one way while we aim another, toward what we want to leave? Something fights our spirit and won't let us want anything for good. We swerve between plans; no wish is free, whole, or lasting.
items.core_idea: We swerve between plans; no wish lasts.

items.plain: Some natures, like buildings on firm ground, rise easily; others must first sink foundations through soft soil, hidden work that is the larger part. Luckier is one never troubled by himself; worthier is one who wrestled his way to wisdom.
items.core_idea: Wisdom won through struggle deserves more credit.

items.plain: Choose as your guide someone you admire more when you watch them act than when you hear them speak.
items.core_idea: Choose guides whose actions outshine their words.

items.plain: How foolish to leave a lecture happy just because ignorant people applauded. Why enjoy praise from people you yourself can't praise?
items.core_idea: Don't value praise from those you don't respect.

items.plain: Why won't anyone admit their faults? Because they are still in their grip. Only someone awake can tell their dream, so confessing your wrongs shows a sound mind.
items.core_idea: Admitting faults shows you've woken from them.

items.plain: What a privilege, to have a human's weaknesses and a god's calm. Philosophy's power to soften the blows of chance is beyond belief.
items.core_idea: Philosophy softens the blows of chance.

items.plain: Death is non-existence, which I already know from before my birth, when I felt nothing. A lamp is no worse off put out than before it was lit; we too are lit and put out, with peace on either side.
items.core_idea: Death is like the peace before birth.

items.plain: I won't be frightened at the last hour; I'm prepared. Admire someone who enjoys living yet doesn't mind dying. The wise man is never thrust out, because he willingly does what necessity is about to force on him.
items.core_idea: Willingly accept what necessity will force anyway.

items.plain: Where you live adds little to peace of mind; the mind must make everything agreeable to itself. I have seen people gloomy in a lovely villa, and others busy and engaged in complete solitude.
items.core_idea: Peace of mind comes from the mind, not the place.

items.plain: You can talk with absent friends whenever you like, and enjoy it more for the absence; presence makes us take them for granted. We're often apart even when together. Keep a friend in your spirit, and they're never absent.
items.core_idea: A friend held in the spirit is never absent.

items.plain: Night doesn't chase our troubles away; it brings them into view and only changes the shape of our worries. Sleepless hours can be as harrowing as the day. Real calm is what a healthy mind reaches when it relaxes.
items.core_idea: Real calm comes from a healthy mind, not silence.

items.plain: Picture a man who silences his whole house to sleep, yet tosses and turns, hearing sounds that aren't there. His soul is in uproar and needs soothing. A still body doesn't mean a peaceful soul; sometimes quiet means disquiet.
items.core_idea: Outer quiet can hide inner turmoil.

items.plain: You can be sure you're at peace with yourself when no noise reaches you, and no words, whether flattery, threats, or empty buzzing, shake you out of yourself.
items.core_idea: Inner peace is not being shaken by words.

items.plain: No one stays the same from youth to age, or even day to day; like Heraclitus's river, we keep flowing. It is madness to cling to the fleeting body and fear dying once, when our former selves die every moment.
items.core_idea: We change every day; why fear one final change?

items.plain: We are weak, watery creatures standing among unreal things, so let us turn our minds to what is everlasting.
items.core_idea: Turn your mind to what is everlasting.

items.plain: Simple living can carry you to old age, which should be neither refused nor craved. There is pleasure in keeping your own company as long as possible, once you have made yourself worth enjoying.
items.core_idea: Make yourself good company for your old age.

items.plain: We are chained by vices we've long wallowed in, not just stained but dyed by them. Folly grips us because we don't fight hard enough for salvation or take the words of the wise to heart; we treat it lightly.
items.core_idea: Folly grips us because we fight it half-heartedly.

items.plain: What hinders us most is being too pleased with ourselves. We accept any flattery as our due, even praise for virtues we plainly lack, like a torturer called 'most gentle'. Thinking ourselves the best, we refuse to be reformed.
items.core_idea: Self-satisfaction stops us from improving.

items.plain: The wise are joyful and calm, living like the gods. If you're never downcast or anxious about the future and your soul stays even and content, you have the greatest good. Seeking joy through riches and titles brings only grief.
items.core_idea: Seeking joy in riches and titles brings grief.

items.plain: Such people chase joy without knowing where lasting joy lies: in feasting, honours, lovers, or showy learning. All are misled by brief, deceptive delights, like drunkenness, which buys one wild hour with days of sickness, or costly applause.
items.core_idea: Brief pleasures deceive us and cost dearly.

items.plain: How little nature needs to be satisfied! A very small amount sends her away content. It isn't our stomach's real hunger that costs so much, but our anxious cravings.
items.core_idea: Nature needs little; cravings cost us dearly.

items.plain: Let us stop wanting what we have long wanted; in old age I no longer desire what I did as a boy. My one task is ending my chronic faults. I live each day as complete, perhaps my last.
items.core_idea: Live each day as a complete life.

items.plain: Before I was old, I tried to live well; now that I'm old, I'll try to die well, and dying well means dying gladly. Make sure you never do anything unwillingly.
items.core_idea: Live well, then die well and gladly.

items.plain: What is forced on you if you resist isn't forced if you want it. Acting against your will, not under orders, makes us unhappy. So train your mind to want what circumstances demand, and to face your end without sadness.
items.core_idea: Want what circumstances demand, and you're free.

items.plain: Prepare for death before preparing for life. Life has enough, but we always feel something missing. Whether you've lived long enough depends on your mind, not your years. I have lived long enough, had my fill, and await death.
items.core_idea: Living long enough depends on the mind, not years.

items.plain: People who claim business keeps them from study are fooling us; their appointments are mostly with themselves. My time is free and I'm my own master anywhere, because I lend myself to my affairs rather than surrendering to them.
items.core_idea: Lend yourself to your affairs; don't surrender.

items.plain: Anyone can despise everything, but no one can own everything. The shortest road to riches is to despise riches.
items.core_idea: The shortest road to riches is despising them.

items.plain: I'm sorry your friend has died, but don't grieve more than is fitting. Not mourning at all is better but fits only someone far above fortune, and even he feels a sting. Moderate tears are forgivable. Weep, but don't wail.
items.core_idea: We may weep, but we must not wail.

items.plain: Will you forget your friend? If your memory lasts only as long as your grief, it's short-lived; soon something will make you laugh. Once you stop watching yourself suffer, sorrow fades, and the sharper it is, the sooner it ends.
items.core_idea: Grief fades once you stop watching it.

items.plain: Let us make the memory of those we have lost a pleasant one. Names of loved ones we've lost will always return with a sting, but there is pleasure even in that sting.
items.core_idea: Remembering the lost stings, yet brings pleasure.

items.plain: Thinking of my dead friends is sweet to me. I had them knowing I would one day lose them, and I have lost them as if I still have them.
items.core_idea: Love friends knowing you'll lose them; keep them after.

items.plain: Let us enjoy our friends eagerly, since we don't know how long we'll have them. Think how often we're apart on journeys, or fail to meet even when nearby; we lose too much of their time while they live.
items.core_idea: Enjoy friends now; time with them is short.

items.plain: If other friends can't console us for losing one, we wrong them. If we have no others, we've hurt ourselves more than Fortune has: she took one friend, but we robbed ourselves of every friend we never made.
items.core_idea: Unmade friendships are a loss we cause ourselves.

items.plain: You have buried someone you loved; look around for someone to love. It is better to replace your friend than to weep for him.
items.core_idea: After loss, look for someone new to love.

items.plain: Time ends grief even if we don't. But for a sensible person, the most shameful cure for sorrow is growing tired of it. Better to leave grief than have grief leave you; stop soon, since no one can grieve long.
items.core_idea: Leave grief before grief leaves you.

items.plain: Reflect now not only that everything is mortal, but that death follows no fixed schedule. Whatever can happen at any time can happen today.
items.core_idea: Whatever can happen any day can happen today.

items.plain: Much remains to be done and always will, and someone born a thousand ages from now will still have the chance to add something.
items.core_idea: There will always be more to discover.

items.plain: Craftsmen straining their eyes in poor light step outside to rest them in daylight. So the soul, shut up in the dark house of the body, seeks the open sky whenever it can and finds rest in contemplating the universe.
items.core_idea: The soul rests by contemplating the universe.

items.plain: The wise person is tied to the body but lives by his better self, thinking of lofty things. He treats life as a term of service, neither loving nor hating it, enduring a mortal lot, knowing a greater one awaits.
items.core_idea: Treat life as service, neither loved nor hated.

items.plain: Let us be brave in danger and not fear wrongs, wounds, chains or poverty. Death is either an end or a change. Ceasing to exist is like never beginning; and if I change state, I'll never be this cramped again.
items.core_idea: Death is an end or a change; neither is fearful.

items.plain: A great person can come from a hovel, and a beautiful, great soul from an ugly, frail body. Nature seems to make such people to prove virtue can be born anywhere, letting them break through their bodily limits.
items.core_idea: A great soul can live in any body.

items.plain: Every honourable act is done willingly. Mix in reluctance, complaint, cowardice or fear and it loses its best quality, self-approval. What isn't free can't be honourable, because fear is slavery.
items.core_idea: Honour must be free; fear is slavery.

items.plain: Annoyance, pain and hardship don't matter, because virtue overcomes them. As the sun outshines lesser lights, virtue's greatness overwhelms pains and wrongs, making them no more than a storm-cloud at sea.
items.core_idea: Virtue outshines every pain and wrong.

items.plain: The good that true reason approves is solid and lasting, lifting the spirit high. What the crowd praises only puffs us up with empty joy, and what it fears only startles us, as animals startle at the look of danger.
items.core_idea: Reason's good lasts; the crowd's goods are empty.

items.plain: One dies young, another old, another as an infant with barely a glimpse of life. All were equally subject to death; it simply let one go further, cut another off in his prime, and stopped the third at the start.
items.core_idea: All are equally subject to death, at any age.

items.plain: As perfectly clear weather can't get clearer, someone who cares for body and soul, with no turmoil in the soul and no pain in the body, has reached perfection. Extra delights only add spice; peace of body and soul suffices.
items.core_idea: Peace in body and soul is the highest good.

items.plain: Let me say something bolder: if some goods could be greater, I'd rank the harsh ones above the mild and pleasant, because breaking through difficulties is a greater achievement than keeping joy within limits.
items.core_idea: Overcoming hardship outranks restraining joy.

items.plain: I'd rather not suffer torture, war or illness, but if I must, I want to bear them with courage, honour and restraint. So hardship isn't desirable; what is desirable is the virtue that lets us endure it patiently.
items.core_idea: Not hardship, but virtue to endure it, is desirable.

items.plain: Put on a hero's courage and step away from common opinion for a while. Picture virtue as something of great beauty and grandeur, worshipped not with incense or garlands but with sweat and blood.
items.core_idea: Virtue is honoured with sweat and blood.

items.plain: Demetrius calls an easy life, untroubled by Fortune, a 'Dead Sea'. If nothing stirs you, tests you or threatens your resolve, and you lie in unshaken comfort, that isn't tranquillity, only a flat calm.
items.core_idea: A life without challenge is a flat calm.

items.plain: When you withdraw from the world, talk with yourself rather than be talked about. Speak ill of yourself in private, as people do of neighbours, to get used to speaking and hearing truth. Above all, study your greatest weakness.
items.core_idea: In solitude, honestly examine your own faults.

items.plain: With my leisure I'm trying to heal my own sores. My trouble is worse than a swollen foot, and hidden: an ulcer deep in my chest. Don't praise me as one who has escaped life's madness; I've condemned only myself.
items.core_idea: I have condemned nothing except myself.

items.plain: Others will outdo me in public influence, pay, rank or followers, and that's worth accepting as long as I can outdo Fortune. In the crowd I'm no match for her; she has more backing.
items.core_idea: Let others win status; aim to outdo Fortune.

items.plain: Like travellers who set out late and hurry to make up time, let us spur ourselves on. Our age suits this: youth's boiling is past, and faults that raged then are weakened and need little effort to put out.
items.core_idea: Starting late, speed up; later life suits growth.

items.plain: I don't like you rushing from place to place. Constant moving shows an unsteady spirit, which can't become whole in retirement until it stops its restless curiosity and wandering. To steady your spirit, first stop your body from running about.
items.core_idea: To steady the spirit, stop restless wandering.

items.plain: Someone getting over an old love must avoid every reminder, since nothing regrows as easily as love. Likewise, to let go of things you once craved passionately, turn your eyes and ears away from them.
items.core_idea: Avoid reminders of what you're trying to leave.

items.plain: We sail past life, leaving boyhood, youth and our best years astern, until we sight the common end. Fools think it a dangerous reef, but it is the harbour we must all enter; arriving early is like a quick voyage.
items.core_idea: Death is a harbour, not a reef.

items.plain: Want to be free of the body's hold? Live in it as if about to leave it. Remembering you'll lose it makes you braver about departing. But how can someone think of their end while craving things without end?
items.core_idea: Live in the body as if about to leave it.

items.plain: To decide what to avoid or pursue, ask how it serves your life's whole purpose. A painter can't paint a likeness without knowing his subject; you can't arrange details without a chief aim. We see life's parts, never the whole.
items.core_idea: Judge every choice by your life's whole purpose.

items.plain: An archer must know his target before he aims. Our plans fail because they have no aim. If you don't know your harbour, no wind is the right wind. Chance rules our lives because we live by chance.
items.core_idea: Without a destination, no wind is right.

items.plain: Devoted to virtue, you'll find everything it touches a blessing, whatever others think. Torture, if you're calmer than your torturer; illness, if you don't curse Fortune: all supposed ills become manageable and end in good if you rise above them.
items.core_idea: Virtue turns supposed ills into goods.

items.plain: Socrates, who said the highest wisdom is telling good from evil, advised: to be happy, follow these rules and let some think you a fool. Let anyone insult or wrong you; if virtue lives with you, you'll suffer nothing.
items.core_idea: With virtue, insults and contempt can't harm you.

items.plain: Everything has its time to be born, grow and be destroyed; even the stars and the earth will end. All things age, at different paces, toward one goal; whatever exists will cease, yet not perish, but return to its elements.
items.core_idea: Everything ends, returning to its elements.

items.plain: To the luxurious, simple living is a penalty; to the lazy, work is punishment; to the idle, study is torture. We call things unbearable where we ourselves are weak. These things aren't hard in themselves; we are soft and flabby.
items.core_idea: Things seem hard because we are soft.

items.plain: What matters is not only what you see but the eyes you see it with; our souls are too dim-sighted to see the truth.
items.core_idea: How you see matters as much as what.

items.plain: It's no wonder that someone stays steady in calm weather. Save your wonder for the person who rises when everyone else sinks and keeps standing when all others have fallen.
items.core_idea: True strength shows when everyone else falls.

items.plain: The evil in torture and hardship is the mind sagging and collapsing. That can't happen to the sage; he stands upright under any load and doesn't complain at what can strike anyone. He knows he was born to carry burdens.
items.core_idea: The wise know they were born to carry burdens.

items.plain: The wise man is still human and feels pain; he isn't a rock. His irrational part can be hurt; his rational part holds firm, brave and unconquerable. There lies the highest good; until it's reached, the mind wavers.
items.core_idea: The wise feel pain, but reason stays unconquered.

items.plain: The wise man overcomes Fortune by virtue, but many who claim wisdom are scared by flimsy threats; we shouldn't demand the same of learners. I still urge myself to do what I recommend, and don't yet follow my own advice.
items.core_idea: Learners shouldn't be judged like the fully wise.
